summary: A 1908 stone light on a reef island in Cobbosseecontee Lake, Maine, built and still run by the Cobbosseecontee Yacht Club; the island is closed and the light is seen from the shore or a boat.

access.note: Owned by the yacht club. The island is closed and reached only by boat.

events.note: Erected by the Cobbosseecontee Yacht Club on a reef island; work began in summer 1908 after a wall was built in autumn 1907.
Steady light in the tower when the Boston Globe report was written in 1908; the club planned a flashing light for the next year.
Steady white light replaced by two revolving oil lamps, white and red, that flash as their reflectors turn; weights drive the mechanism.
A wind-powered generator ran an electric light in the lantern room for a period in the 1930s.
A severe list in the tower was corrected.
New marine-grade aluminum lantern top replaced a wooden one; rededicated 16 July 2005.
Bronze donor plaque installed on the tower, the centenary year.

keepers.note: Commodore of the Cobbosseecontee Yacht Club. The 2005 association history calls him 'Keeper of the Light' at the rededication; it does not give the span of his service as keeper.

corrections.why: Misspelled in the record ('Yatch'); the club and USLHS spell it 'Yacht'.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1908 Boston Globe report, quoted by Forest and Stream, names Frank Morse of the Boston Lighthouse Engineer's office as designer; the 1909 club report names only that office; the 1983 nomination lists the builder as unknown; LighthouseFriends calls Morse a Boston architect whom Robinson hired (cite 7). The designer attribution is therefore a single 1908 newspaper report and a secondary page's version, and is marked as such in the story.

notes_for_editor: Height disagrees: the nomination says approximately 20 ft; the 1908 Globe report (via Forest and Stream) gives about 16 ft of stone plus about 9 ft of wooden lantern frame; the 1909 club report gives a tower of nine feet diameter (its height is OCR-garbled, not quoted). Tenure disagrees: the 1909 club report says a 99-year lease; the 1908 Globe says deeded for 99 years. Builder disagrees: the 1908 Globe names Frank Morse; the 1909 report names only the Boston office; the nomination says unknown. Caretaker disagrees: LighthouseFriends says the Cobbosseecontee Lake Association maintains the lighthouse; the club's About page says the club preserves and maintains it; the USLHS record gives the club as owner and manager. The story gives ownership to the club as the USLHS record and the club say, and states the LighthouseFriends version. (The Lake Association's history page, read in full, does not say who maintains the light, so it is not cited for that.) The donor's wife is 'Catherine L Farr' in the 1908 Globe text and 'Mrs. Clifford B. Farr' in the 1909 report. The 1909 and 1908 texts were read from OCR (Chronicling America, Library of Congress): the quoted phrases were chosen to avoid garbled words, and 'twenty-five foot' and 'seven feet deep' were not quoted because the OCR is damaged there; the checker reads the same OCR text. The 1881 'several years ago' is undated. The LighthouseFriends page is copyrighted: facts were paraphrased, and only short quotes were used. Wikipedia was read only for leads and is not cited. Not checked: whether the 1983 nomination's 'accessible' checkbox matches today's closure; the Lake Association's 2017 solar-LED remark is not cited because the only source found was Wikipedia. Hugh Stephens may be living; he is named only as the 2005 association history names him, in his public role (commodore and 'Keeper of the Light').
